newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Diana honours Bosnia war dead in Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Diana honours Bosnia war dead in Sarajevo.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana mourned the victims of Bosnia's terrible war in a solitary visit to a Sarajevo cemetery on Sunday, comforting an old woman who had come to lay flowers at a grave.
As she walked alone amid the rows of graves in Sarajevo city centre, Diana -- who could not speak with the woman -- reached out and embraced her as the woman cried.

The princess visited the Lion cemetery at the end of her three-day tour of Bosnia aimed at highlighting the danger of landmines left behind by war. She has had several emotional visits with families of people maimed or killed by the weapons.
Diana later went to a hillside suburb of Sarajevo to meet Mirzeta Gabelic, 15, who was wounded in February this year as she was walking to a market. She stepped on a mine and lost half her right leg.
In the garden of Mirzeta's run-down brick house, with cows and goats wandering down the mud track outside the makeshift fence, an aid worker told reporters about the girl.
"Her family could not afford a prosthesis and Mirzeta could not move. We found her sitting in her house and waiting for a solution," said Roberto Maryas of the Jesuit Refugee Service.
The service raised $1,000 from Italian donations to buy Mirzeta an artificial leg so she could walk.

Diana, dressed in a pink designer shirt and black jeans, talked with the family for around half an hour. When she reappeared she walked up the track and greeted several small children who were running around outside.
Peasant women laughed as a herd of British photographers and cameramen fell into ditches and knocked stepladders over as they scrambled to take pictures of Diana on the narrow path.

Although she seemed more than happy to have her photograph taken, Diana, 36, at the centre of wild speculation in Britain about her friendship with Dodi Fayed, 41-year-old son of Egyptian millionaire Mohammed Al-Fayed, refused to answer questions about her visit to Bosnia or anything else.
On Sunday afternoon, Diana flew by private jet back to London where tabloids were running front-page pictures of her and Dodi , whose father owns luxury department store Harrods in London.
The pictures showed Diana in a swimsuit locked in a romantic embrace with Dodi.
Her marriage to British heir to the throne Prince Charles, 48, ended in divorce last year after 15 years. They have two sons.

Even in small Bosnian towns, the princess could not escape the buzz over her love life. Over dinner in Travnik on Saturday, a satellite television in the restaurant carried reports from British newspapers.
Diana was invited to Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation by the Washington-based Landmine Survivors Network to focus awareness on suffering caused by mines.

She held several other emotional meetings with mine victims on Friday and Saturday, listening to the problems they face trying to obtain proper artificial limbs and rehabilitation in a country devastated by war.
Diana toured a "mine action centre" in a former military barracks where United Nations officials told Diana that mine-clearance efforts were running out of funding.
Ken Rutherford, the American co-founder of the network who lost both his legs in Somalia in 1993, said Diana would make a "huge difference" to the cause.

Although Diana charmed the victims she spoke with and may have helped raise funds for the removal of mines, most Bosnians -- more concerned about whether the fragile peace in their country would hold -- were indifferent or even resentful towards the princess. State television mentioned the visit only briefly.
